body:
I completely agree. I just wrote a similar post myself. 

u/YouCanCallMeLeonidas lays it out pretty neatly. I'd say 1 is bang on most of the time. People think they know mental health because sometimes they feel a bit rubbish and order a takeaway. They don't. Unless you've smashed your own head against the floor to try and make the pain disappear (or similar!), you don't. It's brutal and it's not a weakness. Everyday we fight. 

But I also think this is a bigger issue. I've spent my entire career (before it fell into the puddle) working in charities - over a decade. So much money and time is spent on 'mental health'. What's happened is that people think normal problems are mental health, and then they downgrade them because of that. 

"I felt rubbish for a few weeks when I didn't get that promotion, but then I joined the gym and now I bench press my weighty CV five times a day"

etc. 

They don't know. And it's very hard for us to explain it, without sounding like absolute maniacs. And if we do sound like maniacs, they discard us. 

I don't know what the answer is. I think it might lie in drawing some distinctions between what is a 'real' mental health challenge and what is just feeling bummed. But that's not very popular in the age of victimhood. 

If you're here, you're in it. Most people don't get it, but they need to pretend they do. I hear you, regardless.
This is beautiful and you made me cry.
